To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
serum IGF‐I is insufficient to restore skeletal size in the total absence the GH receptor.
the total absence of the growth hormone receptor (GHR) results in a skeletal phenotype characterized by reduced bone size.
the skeletal phenotype of GHR‐deficient mice is not rescued by restoration of serum IGF1 levels.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanisms of skeletal growth.
understanding the mechanisms that regulate skeletal development.
the effects of IGF‐I on growth, metabolism, and skeletal integrity in the absence of the GH receptor.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the GHR is required for skeletal integrity, and that IGF‐1 alone is not sufficient to restore skeletal integrity when GHR is totally absent.
IGF‐1 alone cannot restore normal skeletal size in the total absence or complete resistance to GHR.
in the total absence (knockout) of the GHR, serum IGF1 levels are not sufficient for normal skeletal growth and development.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
IGF‐1 is a poor substitute for GHR, which is required for normal skeletal growth.
IGF‐1 is a critical growth factor in the regulation of skeletal growth but cannot substitute for the GHR in the total absence thereof.
the GHR is essential to support normal skeletal development and growth, and that the skeletal effects of IGF‐I are mediated, in part, through GHR signaling.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the GHR is essential for normal skeletal growth, and that the GHR‐IGF‐1 axis is not a sufficient mechanism to restore skeletal integrity when the GHR is absent.
serum IGF‐I is not sufficient to support skeletal growth in the total absence GHR.
the GH receptor is necessary to achieve full skeletal growth, and this cannot be overcome by restoring endocrine IGF1.
